description: Knowledge mapping between posture measurements and possible Anatomy Trains / myofascial line interpretations.
global_caution: Static posture analysis cannot diagnose fascial restriction, pain source, or pathology. Findings are pattern suggestions only and should be confirmed by clinical assessment and movement testing.

line_definitions.Superficial Back Line: A posterior Anatomy Trains line model connecting plantar foot structures, calves, hamstrings, sacral region, spinal extensors, and posterior head tissues. In posture reports, it may be referenced for posterior-chain loading patterns only, not as a diagnosis.
line_definitions.Superficial Front Line: An anterior Anatomy Trains line model connecting the anterior lower leg, quadriceps region, anterior trunk, sternum, and anterior neck. In posture reports, it may be referenced for anterior-chain loading patterns only.
line_definitions.Lateral Line: A lateral Anatomy Trains line model relating the lateral foot and leg, iliotibial tract region, lateral pelvis, lateral trunk, ribs, and neck. In posture reports, it may be referenced for side-bending, frontal-plane balance, or left-right loading patterns.
line_definitions.Spiral Line: A rotational Anatomy Trains line model linking foot, leg, pelvis, trunk, scapular, and neck relationships. In posture reports, it may be referenced for rotational asymmetry and cross-body compensation patterns.
line_definitions.Functional Lines: An Anatomy Trains line model describing cross-body force-transfer relationships between shoulder girdle, trunk, pelvis, and lower limb. In posture reports, it may be referenced for diagonal loading and sport-related force transfer.
line_definitions.Deep Front Line: A deep Anatomy Trains line model relating inner foot, deep leg, adductors, pelvis, psoas/diaphragm region, deep neck, and jaw-related structures. In posture reports, it may be referenced for deep support, breath-posture relationships, and axial organization.
line_definitions.Arm Lines: An Anatomy Trains grouping of superficial and deep arm continuities connecting the trunk and shoulder girdle with the upper limb. In posture reports, arm-line references are positioning hypotheses only.
line_definitions.Deep Front Arm Line: An Anatomy Trains arm-line model connecting the anterior chest and clavipectoral region through the medial arm toward the hand. In posture reports, it may be referenced for chest-shoulder-arm positioning only.

Superficial Front Line.anatomical_pathway: Anterior continuity from the top of the foot and anterior lower leg through the quadriceps region, anterior trunk, sternum, and sternocleidomastoid region toward the skull.
Superficial Front Line.relationship: A visible sagittal or anterior-chain pattern may be consistent with altered balance between the front of the trunk, sternum, anterior neck, and the opposing posterior line.
Superficial Front Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can be used to ask whether anterior trunk or neck positioning accompanies the observed pattern, without assuming tissue shortening.
limitations: A static photograph cannot establish shortening, downward pull, muscle activity, breathing restriction, or causation within this line.

Superficial Back Line.anatomical_pathway: Posterior continuity from plantar foot structures through the calves, posterior thigh, sacral connection, spinal extensors, nuchal region, and posterior head tissues.
Superficial Back Line.relationship: A visible posterior support or sagittal-balance pattern may be consistent with increased support demand along the posterior neck and trunk portions of this line model.
Superficial Back Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can be used to ask whether posterior head, spinal, pelvic, or lower-limb positioning accompanies the observation.
limitations: The image cannot establish erector or suboccipital activity, fascial creep, tissue stiffness, shortening, or load.

Deep Front Line.anatomical_pathway: Deep continuity from the inner foot and deep lower leg through adductors, pelvic structures, psoas and diaphragm regions, thoracic inlet, deep cervical structures, and jaw-related tissues.
Deep Front Line.relationship: A visible stacking or axial-support pattern may be consistent with a change in how deep foot, pelvic, respiratory-trunk, and cervical regions are organised.
Deep Front Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide questions about axial support, comfortable breathing, inner-leg organisation, and deep neck control during movement testing.
limitations: A photograph cannot determine deep cervical activation, diaphragm function, intra-abdominal pressure, weakness, or fascial restriction.

Lateral Line.anatomical_pathway: Lateral continuity from the outer foot and lower leg through the lateral thigh and pelvis, lateral abdominal wall, ribs, and lateral neck toward the skull.
Lateral Line.relationship: A visible tilt, shift, side-bend, or left-right balance pattern may be consistent with asymmetric organisation along one or both lateral continuities.
Lateral Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide comparison of side-to-side trunk, pelvis, rib, shoulder, and neck behaviour during movement.
limitations: The image cannot establish which side is short, tight, weak, painful, or driving the pattern.

Spiral Line.anatomical_pathway: Cross-body and rotational continuity linking the skull and neck with the scapular region, rib cage, abdominal wall, pelvis, thigh, lower leg, and foot.
Spiral Line.relationship: A visible rotational, diagonal, or cross-body asymmetry may be consistent with a broader spiral organisation rather than an isolated regional issue.
Spiral Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide comparison of head, rib-cage, scapular, pelvic, knee, and foot rotation during movement.
limitations: A 2D image cannot establish transverse-plane rotation accurately, chest binding, tissue tension, or a causal cross-body chain.

Functional Lines.anatomical_pathway: Diagonal continuities connecting shoulder girdle and trunk regions with the opposite or same-side pelvis and lower limb through anterior, posterior, and ipsilateral pathways.
Functional Lines.relationship: A visible diagonal shoulder-pelvis or trunk-limb pattern may be consistent with a cross-body positioning strategy described by the Functional Line model.
Functional Lines.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide observation of contralateral reaching, rotation, gait, and sport-specific force-transfer tasks.
limitations: Static posture cannot demonstrate force transmission, loading direction, power, activation, or sport performance through these lines.

Arm Lines.anatomical_pathway: Superficial and deep anterior and posterior continuities connecting the chest, shoulder girdle, upper arm, forearm, and hand.
Arm Lines.relationship: A visible shoulder, elbow, wrist, or arm-carriage asymmetry may be consistent with an arm-line positioning strategy linked to the trunk and scapular region.
Arm Lines.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide comparison of comfortable reaching, scapular movement, arm rotation, and side-to-side upper-limb organisation.
limitations: A resting image cannot establish nerve status, muscle activation, shoulder pathology, tissue shortening, or functional arm capacity.

Deep Front Arm Line.anatomical_pathway: Anterior chest and clavipectoral continuity through pectoralis minor and the coracoid region into the medial upper limb toward the hand.
Deep Front Arm Line.relationship: When forward head and forward shoulder observations coexist, this model may help frame a chest-shoulder tethering hypothesis that requires movement confirmation.
Deep Front Arm Line.possible_compensation_role: The model can guide observation of scapular posterior tilt, comfortable arm elevation, chest expansion, and whether head position changes with supported shoulder movement.
limitations: The image cannot establish pectoralis-minor shortness, scapular restriction, chest mobility, breathing limitation, or a treatment target.

structure_definitions.sacrotuberous ligament: A posterior pelvic ligament relevant to sacrum, pelvis, and posterior-chain force transmission. Static posture can only suggest possible loading relationships.
structure_definitions.plantar fascia: A plantar foot connective tissue structure involved in arch support and force transfer through the foot. Static visual analysis cannot confirm plantar fascia restriction.
structure_definitions.Achilles tendon: A posterior ankle tendon connecting calf complex force to the heel. Visual heel or ankle alignment may suggest possible loading patterns but cannot diagnose tendon status.
structure_definitions.hamstrings: Posterior thigh muscles that cross the hip and knee and relate to posterior-chain posture and pelvic position. Static posture cannot determine hamstring tightness or weakness.
structure_definitions.thoracolumbar fascia: A broad posterior trunk fascial structure involved in force transfer between trunk, pelvis, and shoulder/hip regions. Static posture may suggest possible loading relationships only.
structure_definitions.iliotibial band: A lateral thigh fascial structure relating hip, thigh, and knee mechanics. Static posture cannot confirm IT band tension.
structure_definitions.abdominal fascia: Connective tissue layers of the abdominal wall involved in trunk support and force transfer. Static posture can only suggest possible abdominal-wall loading patterns.
structure_definitions.adductors: Medial thigh muscles and fascial tissues related to hip position, pelvis support, and Deep Front Line relationships. Static posture cannot confirm adductor restriction.
structure_definitions.pelvic floor: A deep pelvic support system relevant to pelvic organization, breathing, and pressure management. Static posture cannot assess pelvic floor function directly.
structure_definitions.diaphragm: Primary breathing muscle and deep trunk support structure related to rib cage, spine, and pressure regulation. Static posture cannot determine diaphragm function.
structure_definitions.cervical fascia: Connective tissue structures of the neck region that may relate to head, jaw, and thoracic posture. Static posture cannot identify specific cervical fascia restriction.
